analytic.title: Self-Triggered Controllers, Resource Sharing, and Hard Guarantees

div.p: Today, many control applications in embedded and cyber-physical systems are implemented on shared platforms, alongside other hard real-time or safety-critical applications. Having the resource shared among several applications, to provide hard guarantees, it is required to identify the amount of resource needed for each application. This is rather straightforward when the platform is shared among periodic control and periodic real-time applications.

In the case of event-triggered and self-triggered controllers, however, the execution patterns and, in turn, the resource usage are not clear. Therefore, a major implementation challenge, when the platform is shared with selftriggered controllers, is to provide hard and efficient stability and schedulability guarantees for other applications. In this paper, we identify certain execution patterns for selftriggered controllers, using which we are able to provide hard and efficient stability guarantees for periodic control applications.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION AND RELATED WORK
div.p: Today, many embedded and cyber-physical systems comprise several applications sharing the same platform (see Figure 1). Notable examples of these applications are hard real-time, safety-critical, and control applications. The competition for execution among these applications on the shared platform poses several challenges in terms of system design and analysis. In particular, providing hard schedulability guarantees for real-time and safety-critical applications and hard stability guarantees for control applications in such settings is a major challenge.

The schedulability analysis for real-time tasks has been discussed for almost half a century in the real-time systems area, starting with [1]. The design and analysis of embedded control systems have been investigated for more than two decades [2]- [11], if we limit our attention to the traditional periodic controllers.

The novel event-triggered and self-triggered schemes are being actively considered as substitutes of traditional periodic controllers. In the event-triggered control paradigm, the state of the plant is constantly monitored and the plant is only controlled when the expected performance is about to be violated. In the self-triggered control scheme [12], as opposed to constant monitoring of the plant, at each execution instant, in addition to computing the control input, the controller also computes the next instant at which a new control input should be applied in order to guarantee the required control performance.

One advantage of the event-triggered and self-triggered sampling and control is less resource usage compared to the traditional periodic controllers, since the controllers execute only if it is necessary to satisfy the expected performance [13]. While this paradigm often leads to a better resource efficiency, the lack of clear execution patterns makes it difficult to provide any kind of hard guarantees on shared platforms, while also exploiting the potential benefits of the event-triggered and self-triggered control in terms of resource usage.

The theory underlying the non-periodic (event-triggered and self-triggered) control paradigm is now well developed, assuming dedicated execution platforms [12]- [19]. However, the efficient and safe implementation of such controllers on shared platforms is still an open problem, despite several attempts [20]- [26].
Cervin and Henningsson [22] discuss the suitability of different medium access schemes for the implementation of time-triggered and event-triggered control paradigms.

Lemmon et al. [20] consider online scheduling of selftriggered controllers using elastic scheduling, but no stability guarantees are provided. Samii et al. [24] discuss dynamic scheduling of self-triggered controllers, with an objective function which considers both control quality and resource usage. However, the existence of such a dynamic schedule is only guaranteed under a very restrictive condition.

Velasco et al. [21] discuss the challenging task of offline schedulability analysis when the platform is shared with self-triggered controllers. However, the main problem of finding the worst-case triggering pattern is left open. Anta and Tabuada [23] discuss the benefits of relaxing periodicity constraints over communication networks. However, to provide schedulability guarantees, the authors consider the minimum inter-arrival time for all possible initial states, which is extremely pessimistic and defeats the purpose of the self-triggered control paradigm.

In [25], the authors discuss an approximate maximum inter-event time for event-triggered controllers, justified by the fact that a more regular execution pattern of eventtriggered controllers leads to better schedulability results for other real-time tasks. Antunes and Heemels [26] found the optimal sampling instants and control inputs in a given interval, but they do not address the schedulability and response-time analysis problem. Finally, it has been shown that in certain event-triggered schemes no positive minimum inter-event time can be guaranteed [27].

Nevertheless, current practice [20]- [26] focuses on the schedulability analysis for hard real-time tasks in the presence of self-triggered controllers, and they either suffer from extreme pessimism or do not provide any hard guarantees.

In [28], we propose an offline schedulability analysis technique for hard real-time applications in the presence of self-triggered control tasks, that allows to leverage the potential advantages of self-triggered control compared to periodic control. We discuss the fact that self-triggered controllers actually exhibit certain execution patterns when carefully examined. The approach is based on the idea that the next triggering instant for the self-triggered controller depends on the current state of the plant. In our approach, we capture the dependency between the states of the plant at each triggering point. This means that, for each initial state, the following states are not arbitrary, and exploiting this fact leads to a less pessimistic analysis.

The proposed approach in [28] addresses the schedulability analysis of real-time tasks, which are sharing the platform with self-triggered controllers. To perform schedulability analysis for hard real-time tasks, we need to find the worst-case response time (i.e., the maximum completion delay for the real-time task since its release time). Towards this, the proposed approach calculates the maximum interference by the self-triggered controllers. For hard real-time application, this information is sufficient to provide hard schedulability guarantees.

In this paper, we assume that the platform is also shared with periodic control applications. It is well known that in the case of periodic control applications, in addition to the latency (i.e., the constant part of the delay), the jitter (i.e., the varying part of the delay) experienced by the control task is also an important factor for hard stability guarantees [4], [29], [30]. Therefore, in order to provide hard stability guarantees for control applications, the minimum interference by the self-triggered controllers should be calculated.

A naive approach to finding the maximum interference by a self-triggered controller is to model the self-triggered controller as a periodic task, with a period equal to the shortest inter-execution time with respect to all initial states the plant can be in [23]. While this assumption is safe, such an analysis is overly pessimistic, since in every step it considers the worst possible state for the plant (with respect to the inter-execution time). Using this naive approach, the calculated worst-case interference from the self-triggered controller is considerably larger than what occurs in reality. Hence an overly pessimistic analysis.

Analogously, a naive approach to finding the minimum interference by a self-triggered controller is to model the self-triggered controller as a periodic task, with a period equal to the longest inter-execution time with respect to all initial states the plant can be in [25]. While this assumption leads to a safe bound on the minimum interference by the self-triggered controller, it involves huge amount of pessimism, since in every step it considers the best possible state for the plant (with respect to the inter-execution time). Using this naive approach, the calculated best-case interference from the self-triggered controller is less than what occurs in reality.
This basically means that the analysis based on [23] and [25] leads to overly pessimistic delay and jitter values and, in turn, an overly pessimistic stability analysis.

Here, we focus on the self-triggered approach proposed by Donkers et. al. [31], which is adapted for hard real-time guarantees in [28]. The proposed self-triggered scheme in [28] is slightly modified for the purpose of stability analysis in this paper. We address the stability analysis for periodic control tasks, in the presence of self-triggered control applications on the shared platform. We exploit the fact that there actually exist certain patterns in the execution of self-triggered controllers. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first attempt towards performing stability analysis for periodic control tasks, when the platform is shared with self-triggered controllers, that allows to leverage the potential advantages of self-triggered control.

div.head: A. Task Model
div.p: Given is an independent taskset, where each task is denoted by τ i . The j th instance of task τ i is referred to as a job and is denoted by τ i,j . The computation time (execution time) of job τ i,j is safely bounded by the bestcase computation time c b i and the worst-case computation time c w i . The priority of task τ i is denoted by ρ i . Task τ i has a higher priority than task τ j iff ρ i > ρ j . The set of higher priority tasks for task τ i is denoted by hp (τ i ). For a periodic task τ i the period is denoted by h i .
The request upper and lower bound functions are defined in the following.
Definition 1: The request upper bound function I w i (t) is the maximum number of activations (requests, executions, triggers) of task τ i in any interval of length t.
Definition 2: The request lower bound function
is the minimum number of activations (requests, executions, triggers) of task τ i in any interval of length t.

div.head: B. Plant Model
div.p: The plant associated with a control task τ i is modeled by a continuous-time system of differential equations [32],
div.formula: ẋi = A i x i + B i u i ,(1)
div.p: where x i and u i are the plant state and the control input, respectively.

For periodic control tasks, the sampling is done (strictly) periodically and the control input is updated with some delay when the corresponding control task completes its execution. The control input, then, remains constant until the next update.

div.head: III. PROBLEM FORMULATION
div.p: Given a mixed set of periodic hard real-time, periodic control, and self-triggered control tasks, we would like to find out if all hard real-time tasks meet their deadlines and all plants associated with the periodic control tasks and the self-triggered control tasks are guaranteed to be stable, under the fixed-priority scheduling policy.

In our previous work [28], we propose a schedulability analysis technique for hard real-time applications in the presence of self-triggered control tasks. Therefore, without loss of generality, we only focus on the stability analysis for periodic control applications.
The main challenge towards performing stability analysis for periodic control tasks is to identify the request upper/lower bound functions for one single self-triggered controller.

div.head: IV. STABILITY ANALYSIS FOR PERIODIC CONTROL
div.p: In this section, we discuss the stability analysis for periodic control applications. It has previously been discussed that the latency and jitter in the execution of control applications are decisive factors in the performance and stability of the plants associated with them.

For a given controller and latency, the Jitter Margin toolbox computes the jitter margin (similar to the phase margin and gain margin concepts) to guarantee the required degree of performance or stability. That is, the Jitter Margin toolbox provides the stability curve that determines the maximum tolerable response-time jitter J, based on the experienced latency L. The latency L is defined as the constant part of the delay experienced by the control task. The jitter J is defined as the variation in the delay experienced by the control task.

The solid curve in Figure 2 is an example of the stability curves generated by the Jitter Margin toolbox, where the area below the curve is the stable area. The solid curve is generated for a DC servo process 1000 s 2 +s and a discretetime Linear-Quadratic-Gaussian (LQG) controller, with a sampling period of 6 ms.

In order to apply the stability analysis discussed, the values of the latency and worst-case response-time jitter of the control task should be computed. Formally, the latency and jitter are defined as follows (see Figure 3),
div.formula: L = R b , J = R w -R b ,(3)
div.p: where R w and R b denote the worst-case and best-case response times, respectively.

To perform stability analysis for periodic tasks, it is required to compute the worst-case response time R w and the best-case response time R b . In the next section, we shall discuss the approach to find the worst-case and bestcase response times.

div.head: V. RESPONSE-TIME ANALYSIS
div.p: In this paper, we shall focus on the fixed-priority preemptive scheduling policy. This section gives a brief overview on computing the worst-case and best-case response times under the fixed-priority scheduling policy.

The response time of a job is defined as the amount of time it takes for a job to finish its execution, from the moment it is released. The best-case and worstcase response times are, respectively, the minimum and maximum response times among all jobs of a task.

As we discussed in the previous section, the latency is defined as the constant part of the response time of a task (i.e., the best-case response time) and the jitter as the variation in the response time of a task (i.e., the difference between the best-case and worst-case response times).

div.head: A. Worst-Case Response-Time Analysis
div.p: Under fixed-priority preemptive scheduling, assuming each job of the task under analysis completes its execution before the release (activation) of its next job and an independent taskset, the exact worst-case response time can be computed by the following equation,
div.formula: R w i = c w i + τj ∈hp(τi) I w j (R w i ) • c w j ,(4)
div.p: where hp (τ i ) denotes the set of higher priority tasks for task τ i . Equation ( 4) is solved by fixed-point iteration starting with, e.g., R w i = c w i . For a periodic real-time task, we have [33],
div.formula: I w j (t) = t h j .(5)

div.head: B. Best-Case Response-Time Analysis
div.p: Analogously, under fixed-priority preemptive scheduling, assuming each job of the task under analysis completes its execution before the release (activation) of its next job and an independent taskset, the exact best-case response time is given by the following equation,
div.formula: R b i = c b i + τj ∈hp(τi) I b j (R b i ) • c b j .(6)
div.p: Similar to the worst-case response-time analysis, Equation ( 6) also has to be solved by iteration, but starting from the initial value of R b i = c b i . For a periodic real-time task, we have [34],
div.formula: I b j (t) = t h j .(7)

div.head: VI. THE BIG PICTURE
div.p: It should now be clear that the stability analysis for a periodic control application τ i is reduced to finding the request upper bound function I w j (t) and the request lower bound function I b j (t) for a single self-triggered control task τ j .

Our main task is to find the request bound functions I b j (t) and I w j (t) for each self-triggered controller. Having the request bound functions, we can compute the worstcase response time R w i and best-case response time R b i according to Equations ( 4) and ( 6), respectively. Then, from the worst-case response time R w i and best-case response time R b i we compute the latency L i and jitter J i according to Equation (3). Finally, using the Jitter Margin toolbox, we can check if the stability of the plant associated with this periodic control task is guaranteed, considering that it experiences latency L i and jitter J i . 1For the sake of presentation, in the next section, we shall only consider one single self-triggered task and, therefore, we can drop the index identifying the task. Note that there are no restricting assumptions on the number of selftriggered controllers or the priorities assigned to them.

div.head: VII. FINDING REQUEST BOUND FUNCTIONS
div.p: In this section, we shall extend our previous work [28] to find the request bound functions for a single selftriggered control task. Note that, based on our previous work, we already have the request upper bound function I w (t). In this section, we briefly review the proposed approach in [28] and extend the results in order to obtain the request lower bound function I b (t).

Towards finding the request bound functions, the state space is divided into several convex polytopes. Then, for each polytope, we determine the amount of time that the plant may run in open-loop. This is modeled as a directional graph (see Section VII-A). The second step is to use dynamic programming in order to find the shortest and longest intervals of time with k activations of the selftriggered control task, from which we compute the request bound functions.
Having the request bound functions, we can now perform stability analysis for a periodic control application, as discussed in Section IV.

div.head: A. Extraction of the Transition Graph
div.p: There are three steps for construction of the transition graph, which will be described in the following. We consider a slightly modified version of the proposed approach in [31]. We consider exponential stability, where the plant is guaranteed to be stable after running in open-loop for h time units if

We further assume that the origin is excluded from the state space.

As it can be seen in the above inequality, the maximum time h a plant can run in open-loop depends on the initial state x(0). Here, we would like to find the maximum inter-arrival time that the plant can run in open-loop, with respect to x(0), which is valid for all possible initial states x(0). However, the above constraint is not convex with respect to x(0). Therefore, the problem, as it is formulated, cannot be solved efficiently and accurately. To address this problem, we partition the state space of the plant into several polytopes, such that within each polytope the above constraint is linear.

In the first step, we shall partition the state space of the plant into m convex polytopes. The main idea is to partition the state space such that the dominating (maximum in terms of absolute value) component of the state space vector remains the same in the entire polytope. In this way, the inequality (9) will be a linear constraint in each polytope, with respect to x(0).

The second step is to calculate the maximum time h that the plant could run in open-loop before instability (i.e., violating inequality ( 9)), considering that the initial state could be anywhere in the polytope.

Thanks to the careful partitioning and the linearity of inequality (9) inside each polytope, it is sufficient to consider the vertices of each polytope. In [28], we prove that if the system can run in open-loop for h time units considering the initial state to be any of the vertices of the convex polytope, then for any initial state within the convex polytope also the system can run in open-loop for at least h time units.
For each vertex x(0), to find the maximum time h where the plant could run in open-loop, h is increased iteratively until there does not exist any control input to satisfy inequality (9).

div.head: VIII. ILLUSTRATIVE EXAMPLE
div.p: Let us consider that the platform is shared among three tasks T = {τ 1 , τ 2 , τ 3 }. The taskset data are summarized in Table I.

Task τ 1 is a self-triggered control task, has the highest priority, and execution-time c b 1 = c w 1 = 0.3. The plant associated with the self-triggered controller is identified by the following matrices (see Equation ( 1)),

Note that the eigenvalues of this plant are not in the left half of the complex plane and, therefore, the plant is unstable. Task τ 2 is a hard real-time task with period h 2 = 2.0 and execution-time c b 2 = c w 2 = 1.0 and has the second highest priority level.

Task τ 3 is a periodic control task with period h 3 = 50.0 and execution-time c b 3 = c w 3 = 5.0, and has the lowest priority. Furthermore, for this control application, a and b coefficients of the stability condition in Equation (2) are 1.2 and 30.0, respectively.

Our goal is to perform stability analysis for the periodic control task τ 3 . That is, to check if Equation ( 2) is satisfied. Strictly speaking, we use the Jitter Margin toolbox to check if the plant is guaranteed to be stable for the calculated values of latency L 3 and jitter J 3 . However, for the simplicity of the presentation, we consider the approximate stability condition (2) in this example. Towards this, we first need to find the request bound functions of the higher priority tasks of the periodic control task τ 3 . Intuitively, we would like to know how much the higher priority tasks may interfere with the execution of the periodic control task τ 3 . We know the request bound functions of the periodic hard real-time task τ 2 from the literature in terms of the number of events,

However, we need to find the request bound functions I b 1 (t) and I w 1 (t) for the self-triggered control task τ 1 . We shall now proceed with finding the request bound functions for the self-triggered task τ 1 .

The state space partitioning for this self-triggered controller and the corresponding plant is shown in Figure 4. Figure 4 also shows the transition graph corresponding to this state space partitioning. For example, for node 3 (corresponding to polytope 3) of the graph, the plant will run in open-loop at least for 0.8 time units and at most for 1.1 time units and after that the trajectory will end up either in node 1 (corresponding to polytope 1) or node 2 (corresponding to polytope 2). Now, using dynamic programming, we obtain the worst-case and bestcase request patterns. These request bound functions (or trigger pattern) are shown in Figures 5 and6.

Note that the state of the art [23] models the selftriggered task as a periodic task with period 0.8 to find the worst-case response time R w 3 . However, the minimum inter-arrival time of 0.8 time units can only occur one time according to Figure 5. Based on Figure 4, the worst-case scenario corresponds to starting in node 3 (i.e., having the initial state x(0) in polytope 3), running in openloop for 0.8 time units, and moving to node 2 (i.e., the trajectory ends up in polytope 2). After this, the selftriggered controller executes every 1.1 time units (remains in node 2).

Similarly, based on the state of the art [25], the selftriggered task can be modeled as a periodic task with period 1.4 to find the best-case response time R b 3 . However, the maximum inter-arrival time of 1.4 time units can only occur two times according to Figure 6. Based on Figure 4, the best-case scenario corresponds to starting in node 4 (i.e., having the initial state x(0) in polytope 4), running in open-loop for 1.4 time units, moving to node 1 (i.e., the trajectory ends up in polytope 1), running in open-loop for 1.4 time units, and moving to node 2 (i.e., the trajectory ends up in polytope 2). After this, the self- triggered controller executes every 1.1 time units (remains in node 2).

The above example clearly illustrates the pessimism involved in the existing approaches [23] and [25]. That is, the extreme cases of 0.8 and 1.4 time units can only occur a few times and this is not captured by the state of the art [23], [25].

Having the request bound functions for all high priority tasks, the next step is to find the worst-case R w 3 and bestcase R b 3 response times for task τ 3 according to Equations ( 4) and (6). Then, we plug the worst-case R w 3 and best-case R b 3 response times into Equation (3) to obtain the latency L 3 and jitter J 3 . Finally, we can perform stability analysis by evaluating inequality (2) for the calculated latency L 3 and jitter J 3 ,

Let us now use the proposed approach to perform stability analysis. Based on our proposed approach, the worst-case response-time of task τ 3 is R w 3 = 23.6 and the best-case response time of task τ 3 is R b 3 = 15.9. We plug the worst-case R w 3 and best-case R b 3 response times into Equation (3) and obtain the latency L 3 = 15.9 and jitter J 3 = R w 3 -R b 3 = 7.7. Finally, we perform stability analysis by evaluating inequality (2) for the calculated latency L 3 and jitter J 3 and find out that the stability of the periodic control task τ 3 is indeed guaranteed, 15.9 + 1.2 × 7.7 = 25.14 ≤ 30.0.
Using the state of the art, [23] and [25], we obtain R

Hence, based on the analysis in [23] and [25], the stability of the plant associated with the periodic control task τ 3 is not guaranteed, even though in reality this application is guaranteed to be stable, as demonstrated by our proposed stability analysis.

IX. CONCLUSIONS In this paper, we have proposed an efficient approach for the stability analysis of periodic control applications in the presence of self-triggered control tasks, under the fixedpriority scheduling policy. The importance of such an efficient analysis is demonstrated using a small example.
